Photograph: Indranil Aditya/Reuters View image in fullscreen Cockroach Janta party supporters in Mumbai, India, celebrate the resignation of the education minister following protests over an exam paper leak that affected millions of students. Photograph: Indranil Aditya/Reuters Global education AI cheating, leaked papers and marking errors: how exam protests went global Student unrest sweeps India, Portugal and Mexico as grievances and pressure for good grades in tough job market collide Supported by About this content Deborah Solomon and Oliver Holmes Sun 16 Aug 2026 03.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 03.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google F amilies with teenagers in education know the private, hidden pain of exam season. But this year, what might have been a summer of quiet family anxiety has erupted in several countries into public unrest. Exam-related turmoil has led to mass student protests in Mexico after nearly 60,000 university applicants were forced to resit tests amid suspected cheating , while Portugal’s disastrous attempt to digitise school exam marking sparked the country’s worst education crisis in decades. By far the largest and most ground-shaking incident was in India, however, where an exam paper leak affected millions of students and was linked to more than a dozen students taking their own lives. The scandal forced the education minister to resign , and challenged the government’s hold over its 1.4 billion citizens. Why does this exam season seem to be particularly tense and volatile? Experts say the growth of AI cheating and attempts by academic institutions to digitise examinations are at the heart of the issue. When coupled with the high stakes of good grades in an increasingly precarious global economy, the result can be explosive. India’s education minister resigns in victory for Cockroach youth movement protests Read more “It would seem that exams are getting more fraught on a global scale,” said Dr Sarah Eaton of the Werklund School of Education at the University of Calgary. “The pressure on young people has absolutely changed. “We’ve seen the economic situation change around the world in the last decade. And the results of one examination determining a person’s entire future really creates untenable pressure on young people,” said Eaton, a leading expert on academic ethics. “This is a tragedy when young people are dying by suicide because of an examination outcome.” View image in fullscreen Student applicants of the National Autonomous University of Mexico protest over the retake of the admission exam. Photograph: Jose Luis Torales/NurPhoto/Shutterstock When a single test can determine a young person’s entire future, cheating is no longer just about individuals but becomes a systematic issue, said Eaton. This is compounded when illicit commercial industries, known as the “education mafia”, exploit student desperation by stealing and then selling exam papers, something that has become widespread in India and elsewhere. Students from across India joined the mass demonstrations led by the Cockroach Janta party , a youth-led protest campaign that began as an online satirical joke and grew into a nationwide outcry that poses an unprecedented challenge to Narendra Modi’s government. “When you get large-scale fraud combined with systemic failure, there’s almost a guarantee of a breakdown of public trust,” said Eaton. “And once that trust is broken, it’s almost impossible to regain. I can’t imagine how India is going to deal with this, just given the levels of corruption and fraud that we’ve seen.” View image in fullscreen The Portuguese education minister, Fernando Alexandre, whose push to digitise the exam marking process has been deemed a failure with some students and parents. Photograph: Horacio Villalobos/Corbis/Getty Images In Portugal, the national fallout from a failed push by its education minister, Fernando Alexandre, to fully digitise the exam marking process has landed the government in a crisis . Parents, teachers, and students have been protesting, demanding Alexandre’s resignation after his policy resulted in serious marking errors. Similar demonstrations took place in Mexico. The National Autonomous University of Mexico (Unam), the country’s most prestigious university, announced that due to abnormally high marks in entrance exam results, which raised suspicions of widespread cheating, approximately 58,000 students would have to retake the exam. Schools worldwide are rushing to deal with AI use by students, either through bans or teaching AI literacy and ethics to pupils. Denmark announced this month that from the new term, teenagers would have to make a verbal defence of their written essays to combat AI cheating. Eaton has implemented similar reforms in her class. “AI can generate a perfect essay in seconds. So an essay is no longer a viable way to demonstrate students’ learning,” she said. “We should let it die with dignity and find other ways to assess student learning.” View image in fullscreen Narendra Modi’s Indian government is grappling with the fallout from one of its toughest political challenges in years after anger over exam irregularities grew into a wider movement over unemployment and opportunities for young people. Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images In Eaton’s view, cheating is a “human problem” and so grading and assessing student learning has historically also been a human responsibility, which she said cannot easily be off-loaded to the latest tech. But what institutions around the world have been doing instead, she said, is hoping technology can be easily and cheaply used to prevent cheating en masse. Dr Thomas Lancaster, a computer scientist at Imperial College London who researches the educational use of generative AI, has studied how cheating has gone hi-tech. It is no longer about sneaking notes written on a sleeve, he said, but sophisticated communication. Lancaster says students have always cheated but it has become far easier, with pupils using earpieces or miniature cameras, and increasingly, communicating with friends or family with access to internet searches. “I think the number of notes you sneak in, they’re only useful if they’re the right notes and if you can interpret them very quickly,” he said. “But with any kind of communication technology, you can have that expertise waiting outside for you in a human form. They either know the answers; they’ve got the expertise; or they can look them up online. You can go further than that now and have access to AI to communicate directly during the exam as well,” he added. “It’s spy technology, really.” Rather than individual student misconduct, Eaton said the failure to properly train educators was forcing students to spend valuable time trying to navigate through these “broken” systems rather than focusing on learning. “This idea of these mass examinations happening at scale, it sort of dehumanises the learning process and the assessment process,” she said. This, she said, “sort of perpetuates this idea that examinations are the most important thing for students. I think we’ve lost the thread. Learning should be the most important thing for students.” Explore more on these topics Global education Exams Protest Mexico India Portugal Europe features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Education Schools Teachers Universities Students

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text: 'Reform broke no law': Nigel Farage responds to latest donation revelations – video Nigel Farage Farage seeks to shore up damaged leadership as scandal engulfs Reform conference Splits emerge within party after resignation of officials reported to police for apparent plot to evade donations law Rowena Mason , Ben Quinn and Pippa Crerar Fri 4 Sep 2026 14.16 EDT First published on Fri 4 Sep 2026 13.38 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Nigel Farage sought to shore up his damaged leadership on Friday as he attempted to distance himself from two of his most senior officials reported to the police for apparently plotting to evade the law on foreign donations. As the scandal engulfed Reform UK’s party conference in Birmingham, Farage was forced to suspend his closest aide, Dan Jukes, and head of policy, James Orr, after an undercover investigation by reporters from a group called Verbatim . He later acknowledged Jukes and Orr had made “human error” and were “not authorised” to act in the way they did when trying to orchestrate donations to benefit the party from a fake US businessman, who was not permitted to give money. View image in fullscreen Dan Jukes, left, speaks to Nigel Farage before an interview in Clacton-on-Sea in July 2024. Photograph: Hollie Adams/Reuters The Met police are now assessing the evidence after a complaint that Farage, Orr and Jukes may have broken political funding laws , with sources suggesting a full investigation is highly likely to be launched. They all deny wrongdoing. Orr is an associate professor of divinity at the University of Cambridge who had been working for Reform, reporting directly to Farage, since February. In relation to the undercover footage of Orr, a spokesperson for the university said Cambridge was “looking into these matters”. Jukes is Farage’s closest aide who has been at his side for more than a decade working on communications and strategy. Farage had been introduced by Jukes to the would-be donor from the US promising to give £500,000 despite not being eligible, who was really an undercover reporter. The Reform leader then appeared to endorse the scheme for the impermissible US donor to give money through his son, a UK intermediary, by saying “thank you, both” and “all above board”. 11:20 Reform donations scandal: is this the final blow for Farage? - The Latest After dismissing the sting as a “hoax”, Reform began an organised campaign to limit the damage to Farage personally before his main conference speech, after a summer of scandals over his finances including an undeclared gift of £5m . Addressing the allegations, the Reform leader responded by reading out a legal statement in which he dismissed the allegations as “a little local difficulty” and described the reports as “an exercise in entrapment”. Farage claimed Orr and Jukes had merely been “contractors” who engaged in “loose pub talk, including a couple of boasts that simply were not true”. One party figure, Nadine Dorries , claimed Jukes had merely booked transport and carried bags, despite being a senior adviser integral to Reform’s operations and success for many years. View image in fullscreen A man in chainmail and a crown attends the Reform UK conference. Photograph: Sean Smith/The Guardian When it was put to Farage that he had thanked the bogus donors and understood what was going on, he said: “It was the middle of the byelection. I was told I had to go and meet these people. I didn’t have to, but I did. I was told they had a global family trust headquartered in London. I asked the question: is this all above board?” The Reform leader also insisted that the party’s internal processes would have stopped any impermissible donors and said neither Jukes nor Orr should have been carrying out fundraising. He said a suggestion by Jukes in the footage that other foreign donations had been channelled through UK intermediaries was not true and the donors did not exist. The pair were caught out after being filmed by undercover reporters from the group Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, and broadcast by Channel 4 News on the eve of Reform’s party conference. View image in fullscreen Farage’s speech was interrupted by protesters. Photograph: Sean Smith/The Guardian In the footage, Orr and Jukes appeared to help orchestrate an impermissible donation of £30,000 from the fake US donor which was used to pay for polling that would benefit Reform and made front pages of national newspapers. The money from an American company was transferred to the polling company JL Partners after being organised at the behest of Reform to boost its policies and political narrative. It was not declared to the Electoral Commission. Jukes went on to discuss whether the US businessman could give £500,000 through a UK intermediary, who was an undercover reporter, and introduced the would-be donors to Farage at a lunch in Clacton over oysters and champagne. The Lib Dems also asked the standards commissioner to investigate Farage’s conduct. The row comprehensively overshadowed the first full day of the party’s conference with every Reform politician repeatedly questioned over the scandal. It also exposed splits at the top of the party, with Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, strongly distancing himself from Jukes and Orr. He told reporters “anyone who supports Reform is disappointed”, and added of the investigation: “It’s just not something I am personally involved in.” He also launched a personal video about his backstory, leading to speculation he could attempt to run for the leadership as a rival to Robert Jenrick or Richard Tice if Farage were to be forced out over his financial scandals. Reform UK exposé comes just as Farage was hoping to change the narrative Read more However, some Reform insiders are convinced Farage will part company with Yusuf before long, partly over his ambition and combative style on social media, including one post on X that saw him accused of racism towards a Somalia-born Labour councillor. Farage is understood to have used a rude term about Yusuf recently in relation to his troublemaking on social media. One senior Reform figure said they believed Yusuf would have to go as a precondition for some sort of reconciliation with Rupert Lowe , whose party Restore Britain has eaten into the party’s voters on the hard right. Farage has recently condemned Lowe as vindictive but some of their friends believe a rapprochement could be possible if Yusuf were no longer in the party. Reform had wanted the main event to be Farage announcing a deal with the hard-right French National Rally president, Jordan Bardella, to return small boats crossing the Channel if both parties achieve power. However, a press conference was dominated by questions about the foreign donations scandal. View image in fullscreen National Rally ​party chief, Jordan Bardella, attends a joint press conference with Farage on Friday. Photograph: Sean Smith/The Guardian Farage’s main speech was later delayed by security concerns after climate protesters disrupted Tice’s stage appearance – and more activists later repeatedly interrupted his address. While waiting to go on stage, the Reform leader danced and sung with the crowd. He began his speech by calling for Andy Burnham to hold a general election and accusing Labour of planning to put up taxes. Jukes issued a statement: “This was entrapment over a prolonged period of time by individuals using selective editing who had their own agenda to discredit Reform UK .” Orr said: “I have agreed to step down from my current role at Reform UK pending the outcome of the party’s internal investigation into the conduct of the program, with which I will cooperate fully.” The speech was light on policy but Farage at one point hinted he could look at the way judges are appointed in future – suggesting the party could look at a system of political appointments as is the case in the US. Beállítom Mikrobusz és személygépkocsi ütközött Budapesten a Fő utca és a Csalogány utca sarkán, hárman megsérültek a balesetben – erősítette meg a 24.hu értesüléseit a Budapesti Rendőrfőkapitányság lapunknak. A 24.hu olvasójára hivatkozva arról írt, hogy a mikrobusz az ütközés hatására megpördült a levegőben, mielőtt az oldalára fordult volna. A BRFK kérdéseinkre viszont azt mondta, hogy valójában két ütközés történt. A mikrobusz először a Fő utca és a Csalogány utca kereszteződésében ütközött össze egy kocsival, majd nekiment egy másik, parkoló kocsinak a Csalogány utcában, és ezután fordult az oldalára. A 24.hu szerint a buszból egy kislányt, és még valakit szedtek ki a Katasztrófavédelem munkatársai. A BRFK szerint a balesetben hárman sérültek meg, senki sem súlyosan, őket kórházba szállították. A baleset körülményeit vizsgálják, a műszaki mentés még zajlik, ennek idejére az érintett kereszteződést lezárták. Kedvenceink Partnereinktől Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak!
